question.problem:
The function $f(x)$ defined by 

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{x+3}, & x\ne -3 \\ 2, & x=-3\end{aligned}
$$

has an  infinite discontinuity at $x=${{field-1}}.
question.worked_solution:
Infinite discontinuities coincide with the vertical asymptotes of $y=f(x).$ The only possible way that $y=f(x)$ can have vertical asymptotes is if  $-\frac{3}{x+3}$ grows without bound within its respective subdomain.

We compute the asymptotes of $-\frac{3}{x+3}.$ Setting the denominator equal to zero, we get

$$
x+3=0\,⟹\,x=-3.
$$

Although both branches of the function are defined for $x\ne -3,$ we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-3)^{-}}(-\frac{3}{x+3}) & =\infty , \\ {lim}_{x\to (-3)^{+}}(-\frac{3}{x+3}) & =-\infty ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore we conclude that $x=-3$ is indeed an infinite discontinuity.

This matches up with what we see in the graph of $y=f(x),$ shown below.
